caption: ‘s most mysterious project the destiny of baghdad gymnasium is fascinating 1 it’s almost a miracle that it actually exists 2 for many years its existence fell into obscurity in the architecture world 3 le corbusier’s paternity remained controversial for quite some time in 1957 eight of the most important western architects le corbusier walter gropius josé luis sert gio ponti aalvar aalto and werner march constantine doxiadis were commissioned by king faisal ii to transform baghdad into a modern and cosmopolitan capital le corbusier was originally hired to create baghdad stadium and city of sport in support of the citys bid to host the 1960 olympics on july 14th 1958 just one day after the project was formally approved a coup d’état ended the 37year hashemite monarchy of iraq and the king was assassinated most of the largescale projects imagined by the starchitects were instantly abandoned as the iraqi capital didnt get the olympic games the construction of the complex was postponed le corbusiers passed away in 1965 thanks to the support of influential iraqi rifat chadirji a part of the sports city with reportedly little modification to the original plans would eventually be built under the supervision of french architect axel mesney between 1978 and 1980 and inaugurated under the name saddam hussein gymnasium for decades it suffered from the plight of being a posthumous work contested by the purists it was never mentionned in the literature dedicated to the swissborn french architect it was perceived as a bastardized project not bearing the master’s signature while researching for her thesis on modern architecture in baghdad in 2004 researcher caecilia pieri got interested in the complex after years of research in 2012 she managed to put a hand on neverseenbefore construction archives at axel mesney’s proving le corbusier’s authorship the site was renovated a decade ago and is now fully functional it is mainly used for basketball and volleyball games

caption: burj abboud 1955 by 19262020 and abdullah ihsan kamil 19191984 this bauhausinfluenced tower represents the symbol of baghdad intense modernisation and westernisation in the 1950s it was back then the first highrise in town while the includes some vernacular features such as archways screens and courtyards in response to the hot environment it remains mainly a project borrowing to the “international style” built at a time when chadirji was employed by the monarchy mandated under british rule it’s really in the 1960s in a postmonarchy republic that the “father of modernism” will fully express his unique style that he called “international regionalism” the idea was to “combine ancient iraqi heritage with modern art and architecture to develop an iraqi aesthetic that was not only unique to iraq but also influence the development of a panarab visual language” with nearly 100 buildings chadirji contributed greatly to define the aesthetics of his country’s public space especially through the 1970s by 1970 chadirji had offices throughout the middle east one of them was employing a young in 1978 at the peak of his career he was wrongfully sentenced to life in prison but was eventually released after 20 months by saddam hussein who was seeking iraq’s best architect to oversee the preparation of baghdad for an international conference in 1982 in 1983 chadirji eventually fled baghdad for teaching at harvard before relocating in the uk where he would spend the rest of his life the burj abboud survived miraculously six fires in 1985 1989 1996 1998 2005 2x it is nowadays partly unused

caption: ‍️ marina started to ride her through the capital of in 2016 as an during festival her pictures went viral and inspired many people men and women to join her for rides in the city marina still organises group bike rides “the idea came to me when i first moved out of baghdad and saw bike rentals my husband suggested to take a ride and i said i don’t know how to ride a bike he told me you did it before as a kid and it is something you don’t forget i went on it and it felt so amazing because it was something i couldn’t do for years i was told off doing it as a woman and when i tried again i felt free and didn’t like the feeling at the same time because i was so proud of myself i was telling myself it’s just a bike i shouldn’t be proud i didn’t like that my country took that little enjoyment that i had when i was little i was remembering my grandfather telling me not to i didn’t understand why but i followed it was not even my bike it was my cousin’s bike i didn’t have a bike in my life the feeling i had that moment made me want to ride a bike in baghdad and i thought what’s going to happen it’s just because people stopped doing things and maybe we should do it again i bought a bike and brought it all over baghdad i remember the first time it was intense i was so scared i could hear my heart beats it felt so amazing i remember at a checkpoint i was riding my bike and i was so scared they wouldn’t tell me off because it’s not illegal but in my head it was something i shouldn’t do i was riding and i saw him and i was trying to return i didn’t want him to say anything what he did he opened the barrier and let me pass”

caption: has always been battling for its own survival against the in the middle age it managed to become a major cultural intellectual religious and trading centre for many centuries the territory of most of presentday was commonly known in the arab world as bilad shinqit the land of chinguetti the “city of libraries” in is heyday it counted up to 30 libraries for a population of 20000 people which housed thousands of arabic manuscripts the work of theologians writers jurists philosophers poets mathematicians and scientists ranging from the golden age of the almoravids in andalusia in the 11th century to the 20th century five libraries still remain and i got to visit one alhabot a center of science religion and mathematics mauritanians and other north western saharan islamic scholars have had a profound impact on islamic culture scholars bearing the title alshinqiti used to suggest strong scholarly expertise a holy city the city was a principal gathering place for pilgrims of the maghreb on their way to mecca it eventually became known as a holy city in itself especially for pilgrims who couldn’t make the long journey to the arabic peninsula a massive tradingcenter desert caravans transporting gold salt dates ivory and… enslaved people across the sahara were the source of chinguettis economic prosperity with as many as 30000 camels gathering here at the same time historians believe that the spread of islam is intertwined with the development of the transsaharan trade as the religion established common values and a sense of trust among traders by the middle of the 19th century most transsaharan commercial arteries dried up replaced by maritime routes a is a place without expectation facehuntermautitania

caption: riding the for 20 hours makes you feel slightly delirious… still trying to process the level of surrealism of sleeping dreaming and having tea on top of 22000 tons of iron ore in motion in the middle of the it is as well a special experience because this 704kmlong played an essentiel role in mauritania’s history to exploit a humongous iron ore deposit in the deep desert a european conglomerate miferma created in the 1950s a city from scratch and built this to carry the raw mineral to the port of nouadhibou from where it is exported it provided the income for mauritanias economic development and rapid urbanisation during the first two decades of its independence 1960s1970s in 1966 after only three years of operations iron mining contributed to 28 of the gdp and accounted for 92 of the value of all exports during the western sahara war in the 1970s the line became a target of the polisario front who partly destroyed it pushing eventually mauritania to drop its territorial claim on western sahara in 1979 the rail track nowadays briefly crosses the territory of the partially recognized state of the sahrawi arab democratic republic sadr the plays as well the role of a lifeline for many people and remote desert communities who need to travel to visit family or search for work there is one passenger carriage at the very end of the world’s longest 23km and heaviest train but most people ride it atop the iron ore big up to my partnerinadventure for joining me
